newsitem.title: USA: US natgas proved reserve up, oil off slightly - EIA.
newsitem.headline: US natgas proved reserve up, oil off slightly - EIA.

text.p: U.S. proved reserves of natural gas were up in 1995 for the second straight year, while oil proved reserves made their smallest decline in eight years, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said Tuesday.

Natural gas proved reserves -- those that are economically recoverable with current technology -- were up 1 percent last year and replaced 107 percent of 1995 gas production. Proved reserves totaled more than 165 trillion cubic feet.
Oil reserve additions replaced 95 percent of 1995 oil production, leaving 22.4 billion barrels of proved crude oil reserves.
The half percent decline in oil proved reserves was the smallest since reserves last increased in 1987, the EIA said.
For both gas and oil, the EIA said discoveries in the federal offshore, including several in deep water, helped hold up reserves.

For gas, lower prices in 1995 contributed to a long downtrend in drilling. Despite this, the EIA said successful exploratory gas well completions increase by 6 percent to 814. But development and total gas well completions were down.
Total discoveries per exploratory gas well were down in 1995, but still more than twice that of the early 1980s.

Total discoveries of dry gas reserves were 10,961 billion cubic feet, down 11 percent from 1994. Total discoveries, which equaled 61 percent of 1995 gas production, are reserves attributable to field extensions, new field discoveries and new reservoir discoveries in oil fields.
Coalbed methane reserves resumed growing, more than replacing 1994's declines and accounting for more than six percent of 1995 gas reserves

For crude oil, reserve additions from the Gulf of Mexico offset the combined proved reserve losses of Alaska, California and Texas. Lower-48 states crude proved reserve rose for the first time in a decade, and were up 81 million barrels.
Total oil discoveries were 957 million barrels in 1995, of which the Gulf federal offshore accounted for 60 percent, Texas for 16 percent and Alaska for 8 percent.
Total discoveries of crude in 1995 were the highest in a decade, and were 67 percent above 1994.

New reservoir discoveries in old fields were 343 million barrels, which more than tripled both the 1994 total and the prior 10-year average, the EIA said. The Gulf federal offshore had 91 percent of those.
New field discoveries were 114 million barrels, up 78 percent from 1994. Of that 79 percent was from the Gulf federal offshore.
Field extensions added 500 million barrels of proved oil reserves in 1995, the EIA said, 26 percent more than in 1994.
Oil well completions increase slightly to 6,796.
